title: Indo-Pacific and the Quad

cards.b:
For decades the strategic map showed an Asia-Pacific region that stopped at the Malacca Strait. India was at the edge. The new term Indo-Pacific joins the Indian and Pacific Oceans into one theatre and puts India at the centre.

Why this matters to India: over 90% of its trade by volume moves by sea, much of its energy passes through the Indian Ocean, and China's naval presence is growing there.

Exam questions ask four things: what the concept means, India's version of it, the Quad, and the limits of both. Keep ASEAN centrality and strategic autonomy as your two anchor words.

The term 'Indo-Pacific' was used in a 2007 article by Indian naval analyst Gurpreet Khurana. Japan's Shinzo Abe gave it political life the same year. The US adopted it formally in its 2017 National Security Strategy and renamed Pacific Command as Indo-Pacific Command in 2018.

The first Quad dialogue was in 2007 but China protested and Australia's Rudd government withdrew in 2008. The 2017 revival came after Chinese actions in the South China Sea and at Doklam.

At the Shangri-La Dialogue (June 2018) Modi set out India's view: the Indo-Pacific is a natural region, free, open and inclusive, with ASEAN centrality, a rules-based order, and no domination by a single power. He said India does not see it as a club of limited members or as directed against any country.

In November 2019 India launched the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) with seven pillars: maritime security, ecology, resources, capacity building, disaster risk reduction, science and technology, and trade and connectivity.

Earlier, SAGAR (2015) set India's Indian Ocean policy. In 2025 it was widened to MAHASAGAR. India also backs the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP, 2019).

Notice the difference: the US stresses 'free and open' and competition with China; India stresses 'inclusive'.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue links India, the US, Japan and Australia. It has no charter, no treaty and no secretariat. It meets at several levels.

  • Leaders' summits: virtual in March 2021 and March 2022; in person in Washington (September 2021), Tokyo (May 2022), Hiroshima (May 2023) and Wilmington, Delaware (September 2024).
  • Working areas: health and vaccines (2021 pledge), climate, critical and emerging technology, infrastructure, space, cyber, and maritime security.
  • Programmes: the Quad Fellowship (2023), the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA) announced in May 2022, Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer mission and a cancer moonshot.
  • Malabar: a naval exercise in which all four have taken part since 2020.

cards.h: The Quad in a harder year
cards.b:
India was due to host the next leaders' summit in 2025. It was delayed amid friction in India–US ties over tariffs and Trump's ceasefire claims. As of November 2026, no Quad leaders' summit has been held since September 2024.

  • Foreign ministers met in Washington in July 2025, and reportedly in New Delhi on 26 May 2026, announcing work on maritime surveillance, energy security and critical minerals.
  • Reports in 2026 said annual summits were unlikely, with the chair possibly passing to Australia. A possible leaders' meeting at ASEAN-linked events in Manila in November 2026 was reported but unconfirmed.
  • The Trump administration said it still values the Quad, but its focus is on trade and bilateral deals.

Check news before the exam: the status of the summit is the key current-affairs fact.

cards.h: The South China Sea and the Malacca dilemma
cards.b:
About one-third of global trade passes through the South China Sea. China claims most of it under its 'nine-dash line'. In July 2016 an arbitral tribunal under UNCLOS, in a case brought by the Philippines, ruled that the claim has no legal basis. China rejected the ruling.

India supports freedom of navigation, peaceful settlement and the 2016 ruling, though it takes no side on sovereignty claims. It has exploration interests (ONGC Videsh in Vietnamese blocks) and sells defence goods to Vietnam and the Philippines.

The Malacca dilemma is China's worry that a hostile navy could choke its trade at the Strait. India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands sit near the western mouth of the strait. This gives India a card, and explains China's push for ports in the Indian Ocean.

India's own seas: it is building a larger navy, with INS Vikrant (2022) as its first indigenous aircraft carrier.

AUKUS (2021)

US–UK–Australia pact to supply nuclear-powered submarines. India is not a member. It shows the US pays more for formal alliances.

IPEF (2022)

The Indo-Pacific Economic Framework. India joined three pillars (supply chains, clean economy, fair economy) but not the trade pillar.

RCEP (2022 in force)

India left in 2019. China, Japan, ASEAN and others are in.

China's view

Beijing calls the Quad an 'Asian NATO' aimed at containment. It prefers the term 'Asia-Pacific'.

India differs from the US by avoiding a military alliance and by stressing ASEAN.

cards.h: A bulwark or a talking shop?
cards.b:
Realists (Walt, Mearsheimer) see the Quad as a balance against China's rise. Liberals see public goods like vaccines and infrastructure. Constructivists note that the Quad frames a shared identity of 'democracies'. India, however, avoids that label and stresses inclusiveness.

A common critique, by Brahma Chellaney and others: the Quad lacks substance. Defenders such as C. Raja Mohan say its value is in habits of cooperation and the signals it sends.

• Keep strategic autonomy: Quad, plus BRICS and SCO.
  • Build India's own maritime capacity: the Andaman and Nicobar Command, naval bases in Agalega (Mauritius) and Assumption (Seychelles, stalled), the Information Fusion Centre (IFC-IOR) at Gurugram.
  • Use the Quad for capabilities: undersea domain awareness, secure chips and critical minerals.
  • Court Southeast Asia: Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

The test: can the Quad deliver for India while US policy swings?

"The Quad is an alliance in the making. Critically examine from India's viewpoint." (typical)
"Discuss India's Indo-Pacific vision and compare it with that of the US." (typical)
"India's maritime strategy in the Indian Ocean Region." (typical)

Structure: (1) concept: Indo-Pacific versus Asia-Pacific; (2) India's vision (Shangri-La 2018, IPOI, SAGAR/MAHASAGAR); (3) Quad: origins, 2017 revival, activities; (4) other groupings: AUKUS, IPEF; (5) 2025–26 stall; (6) assessment and way forward.

quiz.q: Who first used the term 'Indo-Pacific' in an Indian academic article in 2007?
quiz.w: Captain Gurpreet Khurana, in a 2007 article in Strategic Analysis.

quiz.q: The Quad was revived in 2017 at a meeting held in:
quiz.w: On the sidelines of the ASEAN meetings in Manila, November 2017.

quiz.q: The Quad's last in-person leaders' summit (as of November 2026) took place in:
Modi set out India's Indo-Pacific vision at the:
quiz.w: At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, June 2018.

quiz.q: IPOI (Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative) was launched in:
quiz.w: At the East Asia Summit, Bangkok, November 2019.

quiz.q: India is NOT a member of:
quiz.w: AUKUS includes only the US, UK and Australia.

quiz.q: Which IPEF pillar did India decline to join?
quiz.w: India stayed out of the trade pillar.

quiz.q: The IPMDA initiative of the Quad concerns:
quiz.w: The Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness.

quiz.q: China's common description of the Quad is:
quiz.w: Chinese officials call it an 'Asian NATO'.

quiz.q: Which country withdrew from the first Quad in 2008?
